etymology: Hebrew ābīb, “green ears” or “ripening corn”; the first month of the sacred year, the month of the barley in the ear, in which Israel came out of Egypt; later called Nisan.
biblical_def: Abib is the first month of the sacred year that the LORD appointed at the Exodus, answering to the latter part of March and beginning of April. Its name marks the season of the green ears, when the barley was in the ear and the harvest near. In this month the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt: “This day came ye out in the month Abib” (Exo 13:4), and He bound the passover to it forever — “Observe the month of Abib, and keep the passover unto the LORD thy God” (Deu 16:1). So the year itself was ordered around redemption; the first month was the month of deliverance, and every reckoning of time began from the night the blood was struck upon the door. After the captivity the same month bore the Babylonian name Nisan, but its glory was unchanged. Let the believer mark that God is the LORD of times and seasons, and that He set the very calendar of His people upon the rock of His saving acts. Christ our passover was sacrificed for us in this month; the green ears of Abib were the firstfruits of a greater harvest, and the deliverance from Egypt the shadow of a greater redemption by the blood of the Lamb.
webster_summary: The first month of the sacred Hebrew year, the month of green ears and of the passover, in which Israel came out of Egypt; later called Nisan.

corruption_paragraphs: Abib faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries stands against a secular reckoning of time that has forgotten its Author — a calendar of mere seasons and civil dates, emptied of the memory of God’s saving acts, in which the year turns and turns and points to nothing beyond itself.

etymology: Hebrew zīw, “brightness” or “the month of flowers”; the second month of the sacred year, rendered Zif in the King James Version, in which Solomon began to build the temple.
biblical_def: Ziv, which the King James translators render Zif, is the second month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of April and beginning of May — the month of blossom and of brightness, when the land was in flower. Its great memorial is the founding of the house of the LORD: “in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Zif, which is the second month, that he began to build the house of the LORD” (1Ki 6:1). Again it is written, “In the fourth year was the foundation of the house of the LORD laid, in the month Zif” (1Ki 6:37). So the springtime month of brightness was the month of beginnings, when the first stones of the temple were set in place, four hundred and eighty years after the Exodus. Let the believer see the fitness of it: the house built for the name of the LORD was founded in the month of flowering, a token that what is begun for God shall come to bud and bloom and fruit in its season. The Church, the true temple, is founded upon Christ; and though her building be long, it shall not fail, for He who laid the foundation will also finish it.

etymology: Hebrew ēthānīm, “the month of steady flowings” (of the perennial streams); the seventh month of the sacred year, later called Tishri, the great festal month, in which the temple was dedicated.
biblical_def: Ethanim is the seventh month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of September and beginning of October, and named, it is thought, for the ethanim or ever-flowing streams that still run when the summer brooks are dry. It is the richest of all months in holy days: in it fall the feast of trumpets, the day of atonement, and the feast of tabernacles. In this month Solomon gathered all Israel to dedicate the house of the LORD: “all the men of Israel assembled themselves unto king Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month” (1Ki 8:2). So the temple, founded in the springtime month of Zif, was dedicated in the great festal month of Ethanim, when the glory filled the house. The seventh month was to Israel a sabbath of months, crowded with convocations, that the people might be gathered again and again before their God at the year’s turning. Let the believer learn that the LORD appoints seasons of solemn assembly, and that the highest joy of His people is to be gathered before Him — a foretaste of that great ingathering when the true temple shall be filled with His glory and the tabernacle of God shall be with men.

etymology: Hebrew būl, “the month of rain” or of the falling leaf; the eighth month of the sacred year, in which the temple of Solomon was finished.
biblical_def: Bul is the eighth month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of October and beginning of November — the month of the early rains and the falling leaf, when the year turns toward winter. Its one great memorial in Scripture is the completion of the temple: “in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, was the house finished throughout all the parts thereof, and according to all the fashion of it. So was he seven years in building it” (1Ki 6:38). Founded in the bright month of Zif, the house of the LORD was finished in the rainy month of Bul, seven years complete. There is a quiet lesson in the season: the temple was crowned not in the flush of spring but in the dimming of the year, as the leaves fell and the rains began, that Israel might know the work was the LORD’s and not dependent on fair weather or favourable times. So the believer trusts that God completes His building in every season, and that the true temple, the Church, shall be finished in His own appointed time, every part according to the fashion He has shown, though the years be long and the days grow dark.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the first month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Nisānu; the same as the older Abib, the month of the passover.
biblical_def: Nisan is the name borne after the captivity by the first month of the sacred year, the month older called Abib, answering to the close of March and beginning of April. It is the passover month, the month of Israel’s deliverance, kept as the beginning of months by the LORD’s own appointment (Exo 12:2). In the books of the return it stands at the head of the year: “it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king” (Neh 2:1), when Nehemiah asked leave to rebuild Jerusalem; and in the days of Esther the lot was cast “in the first month, that is, the month Nisan” (Est 3:7). Though the people had borne a foreign name home from Babylon for the month, the sacred meaning was untouched: Nisan was still the month of the Lamb, still the beginning of the year, still the memorial of redemption. In this month our Lord Jesus was crucified, the true passover, so that the very month of Israel’s first deliverance became the month of the world’s redemption. Let the believer see that a change of name changes nothing of the LORD’s purpose; His appointed times stand fast through every exile and every age.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the third month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Simānu; the month of the giving of the law at Sinai and of the feast of weeks.
biblical_def: Sivan is the third month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of May and beginning of June, bearing the name brought home from Babylon. It is named but once by that name, in the deliverance of the Jews under Esther: “Then were the king’s scribes called at that time in the third month, that is, the month Sivan” (Est 8:9), when the decree of life went out to reverse the decree of death. Yet the third month is great in the history of God’s people, for in it Israel came to Sinai and received the law: “In the third month, when the children of Israel were gone forth out of the land of Egypt, the same day came they into the wilderness of Sinai” (Exo 19:1). And in this same season falls the feast of weeks, or Pentecost, fifty days from the passover — the feast of the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, and the day on which, in the fulness of time, the Spirit was poured out upon the Church. So Sivan is the month of the law given and the Spirit given: the finger of God writing on tables of stone, and the Spirit of God writing on tables of the heart. Let the believer marvel that the God who thundered at Sinai in the third month is the same who filled the upper room, and that the law without and the Spirit within are both His gracious gift.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the sixth month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Elūlu; the month in which the wall of Jerusalem was finished under Nehemiah.
biblical_def: Elul is the sixth month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of August and beginning of September, the last of the summer months before the great festal seventh month. It is named but once, and gloriously, in the finishing of the wall of Jerusalem: “So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days” (Neh 6:15). A ruined city was walled again in fifty-two days, in the teeth of mockery and threat, because the people had a mind to work and the good hand of their God was upon them. Falling just before the seventh month with its trumpets and its day of atonement, Elul stands as a month of preparation, a season to make ready the heart for the solemn assemblies at hand. The prophet’s call suits it well: “Turn ye even to me with all your heart” (Joe 2:12). Let the believer take Elul for a pattern: to labour diligently at the work God has given, walls and all, while the good hand of God is upon him; and to make ready his heart against the day when he shall stand in solemn assembly before his God.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the seventh month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Tashrītu, “beginning”; the same as the older Ethanim, the great festal month.
biblical_def: Tishri is the later name of the seventh month of the sacred year, the month older called Ethanim, answering to the close of September and beginning of October. Though the name Tishri itself is not written in the Scriptures, the month it names is the crown of the sacred calendar, for in it fall the three great appointments of the seventh month: the feast of trumpets on the first day, “a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation” (Lev 23:24); the day of atonement on the tenth, when the people afflicted their souls and the high priest went in before the mercy seat (Lev 23:27); and the feast of tabernacles from the fifteenth, when Israel dwelt in booths and rejoiced before the LORD (Lev 23:34). In this month too Ezra read the law before the congregation on the first day (Neh 8:2). So the seventh month is a gospel in miniature: the trumpet summons, the blood atones, and the people rejoice in the ingathered harvest and the tabernacling presence of God. Let the believer hear in the trumpet the call to worship, see in the day of atonement the blood of Christ that alone can put away sin, and taste in the feast of tabernacles the joy of God dwelling with His people, which shall be full and endless in the world to come.

corruption_paragraphs: Tishri faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries answers the modern hollowing of the holy days into mere custom or festival, stripped of the gospel they preach — the trumpet, the blood, and the booth emptied of their meaning and kept, if at all, as sentiment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the seventh month preaches Christ. The trumpet summons the people to worship; the day of atonement points to the blood that alone puts away sin; the feast of tabernacles foretastes the joy of God dwelling with His people. The believer hears the trumpet as a call to worship, rests in the atoning blood of Christ, and looks for the day when the tabernacle of God shall be with men for ever.

roots_lines: Tishri — the Babylonian name of the seventh month, meaning “beginning.”
It is the same as the older Ethanim, and is not itself written in Scripture.
It answers to the close of September and beginning of October.
In it fall the feast of trumpets, the day of atonement, and tabernacles.
The seventh month is the crown of the sacred calendar.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the ninth month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Kislīmu, rendered Chisleu in the King James Version; the winter month of the word of the LORD to Zechariah.
biblical_def: Kislev, which the King James translators render Chisleu, is the ninth month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of November and beginning of December, a month of the deepening winter. In this month Nehemiah, still in the Persian palace, heard the grievous news of Jerusalem’s broken wall: “it came to pass in the month Chisleu, in the twentieth year, as I was in Shushan the palace” (Neh 1:1), and set himself to fasting and prayer. In this month too the word of the LORD came to Zechariah the prophet, “in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu” (Zec 7:1), touching the fasts of the captivity and the mercy yet to come. It was the ninth month, in the cold, when wicked Jehoiakim sat in his winter-house and cut the roll of Jeremiah’s prophecy and cast it into the fire (Jer 36:22-23) — a warning that the word which men burn is not consumed but abides for ever. So Kislev is a winter month of the word: the word that stirs a Nehemiah to prayer, the word that comes to a prophet, the word that a godless king cannot destroy though he burn the page. Let the believer hold fast the word of God in the winter seasons of the soul; it does not die in the cold, but keeps and quickens still.

corruption_paragraphs: Kislev faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries answers the ancient and modern hatred of God’s word — the spirit of Jehoiakim, who sat in his warm winter-house and cut and burned the prophecy of the LORD, thinking to be rid of a word he would not obey.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the indestructibility of the word of God. Jehoiakim burned the roll, and the LORD bade Jeremiah write it again, and more besides; the word men cast into the fire is not consumed but abides for ever. So the believer holds fast the word in the winter seasons of the soul, when the days are short and the cold is deep; it does not die, but keeps and quickens still.

etymology: The post-exilic name of the twelfth and last month of the sacred year, from the Babylonian Adāru; the month of Purim and of the finishing of the second temple.
biblical_def: Adar is the twelfth and last month of the sacred year, answering to the latter part of February and beginning of March, the close of the winter before the passover month of Nisan. Two great things are bound to it. The first is the deliverance of the Jews from the plot of Haman, who cast the lot for their destruction upon the thirteenth of this month: “Now in the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same” (Est 9:1), the day that was turned to the contrary, so that the Jews had rest from their enemies; and the feast of Purim was established to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar in yearly gladness. The second is the completion of the second temple after the return: “this house was finished on the third day of the month Adar” (Ezr 6:15) in the sixth year of Darius. So the last month of the year is a month of deliverance and of dedication — the people spared, and the house of God finished — a fitting close before the year turns again to the passover. Let the believer see the providence of God, who overthrew the lot of the enemy and crowned the year’s end with a finished temple; the same God orders the end of every year, and the end of all things, to the salvation of His people and the glory of His house.

corruption_paragraphs: Adar faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it carries answers the fear that the enemy’s plot shall stand and the year end in ruin — the dread of the lot cast for destruction, the decree that seems past reversing, the house of God left unfinished.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the overruling providence of God. In Adar the lot of Haman was turned to the contrary and the people spared; in Adar the second temple was finished. The same God who reversed the decree and crowned the year’s end with a completed house orders the end of every year, and the end of all things, to the salvation of His people and the glory of His house.
